AMS vendors and Rimini (about 3,100 clients; Rimini Consult): conflicted self-funded transformation, savings sit on rate not units. Integrators at time-and-materials (Cognizant APR agents, A&M cost-out, RGP decommissioning): paid for effort, not dollars out. AI engineering tools (AWS Transform, Copilot, Devin, Resolve AI, Traversal, Tessera): make execution cheaper for the client; the bottleneck is owner sign-off, archive and retention sign-off, contract exit and the budget sweep. In-house (Citi, about 14,000 engineers on Devin): real for the top ~50, which we exclude. Edge: independent, funded, executes, paid only on a third-party invoice drop, plus an underwriting model of realization risk. Watch: AI-native roll-ups of application-management firms selling outcome-priced run; Redress, ISG or Flexera adding execution partners.
result.riskiest_assumption: Once a CFO backs the program, business owners will release at least half of the identified retirable run spend, so that third-party invoice lines actually fall within 12 months. Everything downstream (share, funding, tail, financing) needs a fee base that exists. Price has precedent (SaaS-buying share models of 15-30%, recovery audit, cloud savings share); realization has contrary evidence (20% targeted, 5-6% realized in a health-system panel; $1M of labor to save $200k of licences).
result.two_week_test: 14 days, about $0 cash, no system access, only data the owner is authorised to share under NDA. Days 1-7: recruit one insider advisor (ex-AMS delivery head, ITAM or IT-finance lead); reach out to about 40 people in IT finance, ITAM, vendor management and PE portfolio operations at companies with an estimated $40M+ of external application run spend; offer a free 'retirable spend' list from one export in 48 hours; goal three companies. Days 5-10: from each company's exports (AP lines for software, hosting and support with renewal dates; SSO or usage report; application inventory) build a ranked list of at least 15 units of $25k+ a year with renewal date, usage evidence and named owner; record identified dollars as a share of the base supplied. Days 8-14: the company contact (not us) emails each unit's owner 'we plan to retire or downsize this on [renewal date] unless you object by [date]'; count responses by dollars (written agree, silent, object). In the same window show the CFO or Controller the one-page term sheet (share, tail, buyout, sweep) and record the maximum share they would sign, the paying budget line, the alternative they would use (Redress, in-house, vendor) and which event would make them sign within 90 days. PASS (all three): M1 identified dollars at least 6% of the supplied base in at least 2 of 3 companies; M2 written agreement on at least 50% of identified dollars and objection on no more than 25%; M3 at least 2 of 3 finance contacts state a maximum share of 25% or more on invoice-evidenced lines and name the paying budget. KILL: identified under 4% in two of three, or agreement under 25% of dollars, or finance caps at 15% or prefers in-house or Redress. INCONCLUSIVE: fewer than three companies agree to share data in 7 days (itself a demand signal); then run the fallback of 12 calls with people who ran decommissioning programs (dollars identified, retired and actually dropped from invoices; median realization under 30% means kill) plus two independent counts of qualifying US companies from former AMS delivery heads. Later gates, kill not shrink: day 60 two paid X-rays at $50k+; day 120 one signed program agreement at 25%+ share on a $40M+ base signed by a CFO or Controller; month 6 tech E&O quote of $5M+ with no AI exclusion on human-led work; month 12 first audited invoice drops with at least 50% of Wave 1 dollars realized; miss any two by month 12 and stop.
result.how_critiques_were_addressed: CRITIQUE 1 (vendors concede savings, in-sourcing, contested client levers, SAP, counter-moves). Conceded: rate savings belong to renegotiation; the vendor-labor lever is no longer the lead; SAP custom code is dropped as the wedge; the Big 4 co-sign is withdrawn; ESCO is used only as a contract template. Changed: PRICING/UNIT OF ACCOUNT, fee base is units removed at invoice price (lesser of modelled and actual net invoice fall), excluding rate cuts, AI pass-through and internal labor, so renegotiation and fee work on price versus units and baseline fights go away; WEDGE, dated events (post-merger, pre-exit, platform end-of-support) instead of SAP, top ~50 in-sourcers excluded; MOAT, counter-positioning narrowed to scope removal; AMS lever only via client-signed scope change orders on contracts with itemised exit prices; negotiation-only lines priced at 20% or referred to Redress-type firms. CRITIQUE 2 (volume math, sales cycle, capital, in-house, realization). Conceded and reproduced: the 36-month annuity at 12-15 signings gives 45 payers and $57M at gate inputs, $20M at dossier inputs. Changed: evergreen 10% tail, multi-wave agreements, buyout (the tail adds only about 12%), but the real fixes are PAYER/ACCOUNT SIZE ($40M floor, land-and-expand to about $80M, CFO signs) and VELOCITY (event accounts, sponsor and integration-office channels, 20 signings a year only in the upside); FIRST PRODUCT, a paid Estate X-ray ($75-150k, credited) so free pre-sale cost disappears and cash arrives in month 2-4; first success-fee dollar planned at month 9-15 by sequencing on renewal dates; funding only for units clearing an 18-month payback hurdle; owner sign-off and CFO sweep before funding; the realization gap is now the named riskiest assumption and the object of the two-week test. CRITIQUE 3 (price, capital sign flip, liability, SAP and why-now, moat). Conceded: 30-35% unsupported, so blended share is 26% median and 28% upside, lever-specific; at $30M accounts the model earns about 21% contribution, so accounts under $40M are refused; why-now is moderate; data-library moat blocked by no-training clauses. Changed: capital-light funding gate and co-funded option (model peak burn about $28M median, plan $45-60M); SEQUENCING, low-engineering lines first, non-bank sectors first, SOC 2 early; human-led, AI-assisted work through the client's own change process, scream-test, snapshot retention, liability cap, E&O quote as a gate; MOAT rebuilt as cost curve, our own outcome statistics (an underwriting model, not client data), ledger switching costs and cost of capital. Honest residue: the median is a thin-margin company (about $17M revenue, near break-even by year 8-9), the $100M case needs several assumptions at once (odds about 2-4% unconditional), and the 700-payer count, the 9-11.5% reduction and tech E&O coverage are unverified; the response to that is hard kill gates, not a smaller business.

remaining_holes: Pricing contradicts the pitch. The headline says we are paid against an untreated control group, but the rung-four fee is 85% of the cohort's own 36-month trailing cost, rebased and multiplied by the landlord's rest-of-stock cost index. That is the trailing-baseline pricing the rewrite says it dropped, with an inflation index added. Once a landlord hands over its whole cohort there is no untreated same-profile group left, so a concurrent control cannot exist at the capitated rung.

The claim that the indexed fee does not pay us for what analytics vendors deliver only holds inside the randomised trial. Mobysoft-style repeat-visit cuts land mostly in the hot homes, not in a rest-of-stock average, so the index does not strip them out. Critic 1's cheap-25% point is answered at rung three and not at rung four.

Per-home fee and persistence are inconsistent. Upside revenue uses about GBP2,300 per home, which assumes the cohort stays near GBP2,700-2,800 a year. The pass gate only requires 60% persistence, which implies a counterfactual near GBP1,700. A control-based fee at 85% of that is about GBP1,430 a home, roughly 38% less recurring revenue. The GBP2,800 cohort cost is also self-described as unsourced.

Randomised waitlist controls collide with Awaab's Law. Phase 2 commentary (Clyde & Co and others; I did not read the gov.uk text) says supplementary works to prevent recurrence must start within 5 working days of the investigation, with 12 weeks as the backstop. Withholding root-cause works from control homes for a winter is legally exposed wherever a qualifying hazard is reported, and invites disrepair claims. The rewrite does not address this.

Rung three has no procurement route. 400 homes at about GBP3,000 each is about GBP1.2M, well above the roughly GBP207k-213k services threshold the rewrite relies on for the 50-home sprint. The capitated rung is a full flexible-procedure tender with turnover tests of about 1.5-2x annual contract value, which Critic 3 raised; the rewrite answers only with 'parent-guarantee provider'. Below-threshold relief is real (s.85 Procurement Act bars suitability or turnover gates on regulated below-threshold contracts) and helps rung two, but does not extend to rungs three or four.

The prime channel is declared, not shown. No prime has been asked, and primes such as Wates already sell root-cause fixes with direct labour. At GBP1,900 a home, break-even is roughly a 40% cut with a landlord-funded fix and roughly 55% with a newco-funded one, and the prime keeps the spread. No unit economics are given for the GBP15.2M of upside revenue from this channel.

Capitated economics worsen over time. The fee glides from 85% to 75%, which pushes the provider-funded break-even cut from about 40% to about 48%. The upside assumes a 45% cut, so at year 5 it still loses money if the provider funds the fix. The rewrite's quoted 43% break-even also does not reconcile to its own inputs (I get about 39.5% at 85%).

Buyer pull for the capitated rung has no new evidence. The rewrite removes the uncapped guarantee and puts claims outside the fee, so the landlord keeps the full s10A tail and the saving shrinks from 20% to 15%, which makes the finance-director risk/reward worse. The answer is only that the landlord will buy after seeing its own trial. I found no outcome-priced or gain-share damp-and-mould contract; landlords buy remediation by direct award from Fusion21 or PfH frameworks, where the newco is not listed.

Rungs two and three compete head-on with Wates Healthy Homes (direct labour, root-cause fixes, no 2026 data found) and framework suppliers. A 24-month re-performance warranty is table stakes against Airtech's three-year and EnviroVent's ten-year guarantees, and a free ledger x-ray is what Mobysoft already sells.

Internal sizing inconsistency. The rewrite says a price-per-property book yields a cohort of 500-600 homes, yet the upside has four prime-channel books of 2,000 homes each, which needs each prime to aggregate three or four landlord contracts, each consenting to the variation. The counterparty count of 19 also does not match the stated components (12 + 4 = 16, plus unspecified fix-only customers).
The $17M median is conditional on passing the data gate (30%) and the first trial. The unconditional median outcome is the kill, at zero revenue, so the label flatters the case.
The gate's failure condition conflates two questions: fewer than 2 ledgers by day 28 would kill the idea on a data-sharing failure, which is different from whether the hot-spot cohort exists.
result.which_critiques_were_dodged_not_answered: Most of the rewrite's response is concession and removal. It drops the 80%-of-trailing pricing, the uncapped guarantee, the carve-out and the cornered-dataset moat, and reframes the first sale as a remediation sprint. That genuinely answers the pricing-baseline, uninsurable-guarantee, moat and cold-carve-out objections. It does not answer the two fatal objections for the business that carries the upside. Critic 2 (no evidence anyone buys capitation; buyers bundle and insource): dodged by sequencing. Capitation is deferred until the landlord sees its own trial and no new buyer evidence is offered. About 79% of upside revenue is the capitated and prime-capitated rung, which is the product Critic 2 called unbuyable, and the pull depends on a category-creation step the rewrite itself names as its weakest link. Critic 3 (procurement door, turnover and D&B tests, capital): only partly answered. The below-threshold sprint route is correct and helpful, but it does not cover the 400-home trial or the capitated tender. The turnover and parent-guarantee problem is passed to primes who are unasked and who hold the economics. Critic 1's cheap-analytics point: the fee-indexing answer works only inside the trial. The Wates Healthy Homes overlap is acknowledged but not distinguished beyond gain-share and the control method. Critic 3's why-now point (works to prevent recurrence become a statutory per-case step inside every incumbent's contract) is reused as a demand driver without addressing that incumbents absorb it. Credit where due: the regression-to-the-mean and persistence gate (Camden is the right analog), the explicit no-moat-today statement, staged capital, and the stated 3-5% odds.
result.upside_believable: No. The upside needs six conditions to hold together: a 25%-plus cost share at the top 5-8% with 60%-plus persistence, a causal cut of 45%-plus after a winter, a new outcome-priced hot-spot lot appearing in 2029-33 tenders, GBP20-30M of fund capital raised on a thin evidence base, four primes choosing to subcontract rather than build in-house, and 60-70% renewal with no insourcing. Even generous independent odds (0.5 on the cut, 0.25 on category creation, 0.6 on capital, 0.5 on primes, 0.7 on renewal) put the conditional probability near 2-3%, not 10-15%, and overall under 1% against the stated 3-5%. The revenue arithmetic itself checks out (GBP49.7M + 15.2M + 16.5M + 1M = GBP82.4M, about $107M at 1.3), but it requires about 27% of reachable counterparties by year 7, which the rewrite itself calls heroic. It prices cohort homes at a per-home fee that assumes near-total persistence while the gate allows 60%, and it counts about 20% of revenue as GBP5,500-a-home pass-through works with blended EBITDA of only 8-12%. The credible residual is a small specialist niche: rungs one to three plus a few prime or insourcing fix-only deals, plausibly low single-digit GBP millions, in line with the dossier's $13M median and $58M upside rather than $100M.

result.rationale:
The insight is real and somewhat non-obvious. Repair demand is skewed. Responsive contractors are paid per visit, so nobody is paid to fix root causes. Awaab's Law phase 2 (30 Nov 2026) makes recurrence legally expensive, with claimant costs uncapped to at least Oct 2028. The strongest part of the refined idea is paying against a randomised concurrent control rather than a trailing baseline. That is a genuine methodological edge, the Camden hotspotting analogy is the right one, and a verified-effects library could become a bankable standard in the way IPMVP did for energy savings. The 8-week, under-GBP25k kill test is also admirable.

As a seed deal it is a small business, not venture scale. The pass probability on the first gate is about 30%, and the stated 3-5% odds of reaching $100M are probably still generous. The second-round critic's chain of independent conditions (45%+ causal cut, a new outcome-priced lot appearing in tenders, GBP20-30M of fund capital, primes choosing to subcontract, 60-70% renewal) puts the overall odds nearer 1%. The dossier's own range, about $13M median and $58M upside, is the more credible ceiling. Blended EBITDA of 8-12% is services-grade, since about 20% of upside revenue and much of the rest is pass-through works. The equity story depends on a fund and protocol layer that does not exist yet. The market is UK-only, with roughly 45-55 reachable large landlords, and the buyer pool is bundling into price-per-property contracts and insourcing (Teign, Hyde, Basildon). Few investors would back that at seed.

The rewrite honestly concedes most of the original fatal flaws: the trailing-cost pricing, the uncapped guarantee, and the moat claims. The second critic's remaining holes are serious, though:
- Once a landlord hands over its whole cohort there is no untreated control left, so the capitated fee falls back to a trailing-baseline price.
- Randomised waitlist controls collide with Awaab supplementary-works clocks.
- The 400-home trial is about GBP1.2M, well above the procurement threshold the sprint relies on.
- The capitated fee persistence and break-even maths do not reconcile.
- The prime channel is declared, not shown.

Demand evidence is thin. Landlords pay for works and software (Wigan GBP2M, InCommunities GBP3M), but nobody has been found paying for cohort risk transfer or outcome-priced damp-and-mould contracts. Wates Healthy Homes already sells root-cause fixes with its own labour. Mobysoft already sells the ledger analysis cheaply.

What survives is a specialist remediation and verification niche, plausibly low single-digit GBP millions. It is worth a cheap test but not a decade-defining seed deal.

Score: 3 overall, a decent specialist niche business rather than a venture-scale company.

SIZE OF PRIZE (3). The addressable pool is about GBP570-620M a year of spend landlords already make, in one country and one sub-segment. The pitch's own odds are 3-5% of reaching $100M a year. The second-round critic's independent estimate is under 1%, because six conditions have to hold together: the cost concentration, a 45%+ causal cut, new tenders that price against a control, GBP20-30M of fund capital, primes subcontracting rather than building in-house, and renewals. Even the $107M upside case relies on about 27% of reachable counterparties, which the pitch itself calls heroic. About 20% of that revenue is GBP5,500-a-home pass-through works. Blended EBITDA is 8-12% (Mears earns about 5.7%). The equity story therefore rests on a "fund and protocol layer" that does not exist yet. The credible outcome is a low-single-digit GBP million specialist firm, in line with the dossier's $13M median and $58M upside. No seed fund underwrites that as a venture return. Stripe, Toast and Samsara had a plausible path to a very large outcome at founding, and this does not.

WHY NOW (6). Awaab's Law phase 2 starts 30 Nov 2026. Guidance requires works that prevent recurrence. Claimant costs are uncapped to at least Oct 2028. Sector cash interest cover is 59%, repairs spend is forecast up 14%, and only 4% of landlords call themselves very prepared. All of that is real and primary-sourced. But the same shock raises the cost base, pushes insourcing (Teign, Basildon, Cheshire West, Hyde), and turns root-cause works into a statutory per-case step inside every incumbent's contract. The Decent Homes Standard 2035 criterion is no forcing function. The rung-four capitated market is a 2029-31 event the company would have to help create. So the timing is good for rungs one to three and speculative for the rung that carries about 79% of the upside revenue.

NON-CONSENSUS AND RIGHT (6). Control-indexed pricing, the stepped-wedge randomised trial and the regression-to-the-mean discipline (Camden hotspotting is the right analog) are genuinely sharp. The honest odds and the kill gate are unusually disciplined. But being right is unproven. Mobysoft and Switchee sell the easy 25% cheaply. Wates Healthy Homes already sells root-cause fixes for damp and mould. Price-per-property primes already take capitated risk. Landlords asked to carve out their worst homes are bundling, insourcing, or selling and regenerating the negative-value ones. The final pricing still contradicts the pitch: the rung-four fee is built on trailing cost with an index, and a concurrent control cannot exist once a landlord hands over its whole cohort. The pitch is paid against a control only at rung three.

DEFENSIBILITY (3). The pitch says there is no moat on day one. The reachable moats are a causal-effects library after about three winters and a verification standard adopted by a third party, and both are speculative. The protocol is easy to copy once published, and Wates or Mears could add a gain-share schedule. The 24-month warranty is table stakes against Airtech's three-year and EnviroVent's ten-year guarantees.

FEASIBILITY (4). The 8-week test costs under GBP25k and the staged ladder is smart. But the 50-home sprint is the only rung with a clean procurement route (below the GBP207,720 services threshold, with s.85 relief). The 400-home trial (about GBP1.2M) and the capitated tender face full flexible-procedure turnover and D&B tests that a newco cannot meet. Randomised waitlist controls collide with Awaab's Law, because withholding preventive works from control homes is legally exposed. The prime channel is unasked. Capitation needs a stop-loss that does not exist, and the landlord keeps the s10A tail. Sales cycles run 14+ months. Break-even needs a 40-48% cut when the provider funds the fix, against a measured 25% from analytics alone.

EVIDENCE OF DEMAND (3). Landlords demonstrably pay for damp-and-mould works and analytics (Wigan about GBP2M, InCommunities about GBP3M, Mobysoft GBP97-276k a year). No landlord is known to buy a cohort carve-out, outcome-priced or capitated, and every observed buyer behaviour points to bundling or insourcing. The load-bearing fact, that the top 5-8% of homes carry 25%+ of spend persistently, is unmeasured. Public Thurrock data suggests broad concentration (27% of homes with 5+ repairs) rather than a sharp tail. The per-home fee also depends on persistence. The gate allows 60%, which implies a counterfactual near GBP1,700 and about 38% less recurring revenue than the upside assumes. The idea does deserve credit for its cheap, falsifiable first test.

NET: fundable as a small bootstrapped or angel-backed venture, or as a services-plus-data spin-out. Not a deal a top seed fund competes for.

Score reflects the opportunity as a founder of profitable companies would see it, after reading the dossier, the refined pitch and both critique rounds.

What is real. There is urgent, budgeted pain. Awaab's Law phase 2 starts 30 Nov 2026, claimant costs are uncapped to at least Oct 2028, and landlords already spend visibly on damp and mould (Wigan about GBP2M, InCommunities about GBP3M). Demand-side skew in repairs is plausible. The ladder is sensible: a free ledger x-ray, then a roughly GBP150k sprint under the procurement threshold, then a controlled trial. That is the right way to dodge the fatal "nobody buys capitation" objection, and the 8-week, under-GBP25k kill gate is capital-efficient. The refined version also conceded the right things (trailing-baseline pricing, uncapped guarantee, cornered-data moat).

Why it stays at 4. First, the first customers are plausible but not likely at the 10 mark. Two to four sprint customers in 12 months is believable. Ten is not, because UK housing sales cycles run 6 to 18 months, data-sharing and GDPR friction is real, and PfH itself says pilots rarely convert. Second, the pitch is internally inconsistent where it matters most. Rung four prices at 85% of the cohort's own rebased trailing cost times a rest-of-stock index. That is trailing-baseline pricing, and no concurrent untreated control can exist once the landlord hands over the whole cohort. Randomised waitlist controls also collide with Awaab's Law duties to do supplementary works to prevent recurrence. Third, rungs three and four have no clean procurement route: 400 homes at about GBP3k is about GBP1.2M, well over the roughly GBP207k threshold, and a capitated tender brings turnover tests of about 1.5 to 2x contract value. Fourth, unit economics are thin and worsen over time. Break-even cuts are about 40 to 48% when the provider funds the fix, against a measured analytics-only 25%. The upside revenue assumes about GBP2,300 a home, while the 60% persistence gate implies a fee nearer GBP1,430. About 79% of upside revenue sits in the capitated rung that Critic 2 called unbuyable. Blended EBITDA is only 8 to 12%.

Venture-scale view. The idea states its own odds at 3 to 5% for $100M, and the critic's compounding puts that under 1%. The honest outcome is a niche remediation and verification business at low single-digit GBP millions. The dossier's $13M median and $58M upside describe a decent specialist services firm, not a seed-stage outlier. Moat is none on day one. The aspirational library of measured effects and the verification protocol are years away and could be absorbed by Wates, Mears or Mobysoft, who hold the data and the vans. Rung four also needs GBP20-40M of balance-sheet capital. Managed-care capitation analogs such as Cano Health are cautionary, not encouraging.

Timing is the best dimension: the Awaab's Law catalyst is real and dated, though incumbents and frameworks are absorbing it. Originality is above average thanks to control-indexed outcome pricing and the fix, dispose or regenerate triage. A cheap, fast kill gate and a credible small-business floor stop this from scoring lower. By the calibration scale it is a 3 to 4 (decent small business, not venture-scale), and I land at 4 because the early rungs are budget-funded and cheap to test.

result.title: Covenant Parks (refined: two-tier covenant small-park roll-up)
result.one_liner: A for-profit buyer of small land-lease communities in rent-capped or purchase-right states that records a free 5% rent-ceiling covenant on every park and sells a deeper cap only to state programs and mission capital. After the critiques it is a sound strategy for an experienced operator, not a $100M company.
result.pitch:
Covenant Parks, refined, buys 40-150 site land-lease communities in states where residents already hold purchase rights or lawmakers have capped rent (New York, Maine, New Jersey, Washington, Oregon, Massachusetts) and records a covenant that costs sellers nothing. The standard tier is a 5% annual ceiling on in-place residents, 90 days' notice, no junk fees and a resident right to buy at a pre-agreed appraisal formula. By my rebuild of the dossier's model, that ceiling lets a buyer targeting 10% gross levered (about 7.5-8% net) bid level with a private-equity buyer and roughly 0 to 7% below an institution. A deeper tier (3-4% cap, resident equity credit) is sold only to counterparties with a budget line: New York's MHAP (3% loans up to $60,000 a pad; for-profit acquirers are eligible if they partner for the experience rule), Minnesota-style grants that attach 25-year covenants, and residents' associations exercising purchase rights. Debt comes from community banks and credit unions, as FG Communities finances its small parks, not from agency loans that demand a seasoned sponsor. Equity comes from the channels small-park platforms really use: 1031/DST money, retail preferred and family offices, with a seasoned MHC operator as co-founder. The first product is one park, not a fund.

That is the strongest honest version, and it fails three ways. The version that costs sellers nothing is a label any competitor can copy, and FG Communities already runs this roll-up under a preserve-affordable-housing banner, at about 3,100 to 4,000 sites and $9.6M of 2025 rental income. The version with a moat, a 4% cap, has no payer at scale: parity costs $4.6k to $14.7k a site, $66M to $210M across 14,300 sites, against state money in the tens of millions and federal PRICE funding at zero for FY2026. And scale lives in 100-500 site parks, where institutions set the price; a capped buyer wins only 30-100 site parks, where $100M of rent means 350 to 480 deals. The best case is about $60M of rent by year 11, at FG Communities' demonstrated pace, from a team a new founder does not have. Verdict: a sound strategy for an experienced operator, not a $100M company. Dead.
result.wedge_customer: Independent owners (often one-park, 65+) of 40-150 site communities in New York, Maine, New Jersey, Washington, Oregon and Massachusetts, where residents hold purchase rights or rent is already capped. Preference for parks on municipal water and sewer. Deep-cap (Tier B) parks are limited to about 25% of sites.
result.payer_and_signer: Residents pay lot rent ($3.5-5.75k a site a year in small parks) and pay nothing extra for the covenant. Signers: the selling owner or listing broker (and the residents' association in purchase-right states); community-bank or credit-union lenders; the 1031/DST sponsor, family-office or retail-preferred investment committee; NY HCR's credit committee (or a Minnesota Housing equivalent) for Tier B subsidy loans. Nobody pays for Tier A. No seller, allocator or lender has been found who says they will pay for a for-profit covenant.
result.first_product: One acquisition: a 60-150 site park in New York or Maine, bought with a seasoned operating partner, with a recorded Tier A covenant as a separate instrument (not in the lease), a community-bank first loan, and an MHAP infrastructure loan carrying its regulatory agreement. Not a fund.
result.pricing: Tier A is free to sellers and residents: a 5% annual ceiling on in-place residents, bid at no more than 3% below the best uncovenanted offer. My model puts it at -6.5% to +0.6% against an institutional bidder and +4% to +12% against a private-equity bidder at a 10% gross levered target. Tier B (3-4% cap, equity credit) is priced to the payer. Parity subsidy for a 4% cap is $4.6k-$14.7k a site, so Tier B is sold only to state programs and mission capital. Sponsor economics: roughly 1.5% asset-management fee plus carry, about 5-8% of consolidated rent.
result.why_now: Real but mis-routed. Purchase-right and cap statutes (NY 2023, Maine 2025-26, NJ and WA 2025-26), REIT rent growth of 5-9% and 23% institutional ownership have made owners politically exposed. But statute delivers the covenant for free where it applies, subsidy and tax breaks flow to nonprofits and co-ops, and the rate shock (10-year about 5.1%, 7.2% agency-range debt) hurts a capped buyer most. A why-now that favors ROC USA first is not an edge for a for-profit.
result.moat: None of the 7 Powers is reachable in time. Counter-positioning against REITs is gone: the free tier is a label FG Communities, Sun or any fund can copy at no cost, and the deep tier has no payer at scale. The only plausible cornered resource is Tier B eligibility and track record with state programs (NY MHAP, Minnesota) plus resident-association relationships in purchase-right states, and those pools are tens of millions of dollars. Process power in small-park operations is arguable but unproven.
result.bottom_up_market: Universe: 43,000+ communities, 4.3M sites (MHI via Philadelphia Fed). Wedge supply is small parks: NY registry 1,167 parks, 61,706 sites, median 30 sites, 14% have 100+ sites (dossier, state data); Maine 475 communities, 19,348 lots, average 41; Berkadia counts 460 communities sold nationally in 2025 (likely undercounts small parks). Spend per site-year: US median about $5k (2021), Maine $5,750, FG Communities' Carolinas parks about $3.5-4.5k (my derivation from its filing), Sun $9.2k. $100M = 14,300 sites at $7k or 17,400 at $5.75k = 350-480 parks of 30-41 sites = 0.33-0.4% of national sites, about $315M of equity at $22k a site (about $570M at FG Communities' paid-in-capital-per-site ratio). Reachable payers: parks bought at 22-35 a year, roughly 5-8% of Berkadia's national count. The pace that exists: FG Communities reached about 3,100-4,000 sites and $9.6M of 2025 rental income in about 4 years.
result.upside_assumptions: All of these at once: (1) a seasoned MHC operator is a co-founder, which also satisfies Freddie's two-year sponsor rule; (2) a first fund of at least $60M closes within 24 months through 1031/DST, retail preferred and an anchor family office; (3) the 5% ceiling holds price parity (sellers and brokers take bids within 3% of the best offer) in at least four purchase-right or cap states; (4) community-bank and credit-union debt at about 6.5-7.5% and 60-65% LTV stays available; (5) pace reaches FG Communities' demonstrated ~900 sites a year from year 3 and holds for 8 years; (6) rents grow about 4.5% a year to ~$8.2k a site; (7) two more equity raises, ~$165M in total at $22k a site (about $300M at FG Communities' actual ratio). That yields about 7,450 sites and ~$60M of rent by year 11. $100M needs ~12,000 sites, about 1.6x the only comparable's pace sustained for 8 years, and $265M+ of equity. I put the joint probability of the $100M row in the low single digits.
result.competitors_and_edge: FG Communities Holdings (Nasdaq: FGC): same niche, same mission language, ~3,100-4,000 sites, $9.6M 2025 rental income, public equity plus DST capital, no cap. Havenpark (100+ communities, 30,000+ sites, average 270 sites) and Sun, ELS, UMH own the 100-500 site core. Apollo ($850M first close), GMF Fund II ($250M), 52TEN Fund III and Manufactured Housing Properties Inc. ($100M preferred) are active buyers of parks. ROC USA (361 resident-owned communities, $47M acquisition pool) and its ICS subsidiary (one deal, shut down in 2025 per critic 2) hold the mission lane. NY MHAP (about $24M, for-profit mission acquirers eligible with a partner) and Minnesota grants pay for covenants but are small. Edge: none durable. At best a Tier B subsidy-eligibility track record, thin.
result.riskiest_assumption: That a seller or broker holding a market bid will accept a covenant bid (the 5% ceiling tier) at no more than 3% below it. If they will not, the covenant has no payer even in its cheapest form, and capital, debt and scale questions are moot.
result.two_week_test: No capital and no unfunded LOIs. Days 1-4: list 15 live listings and 25 owner contacts for 40-150 site parks in NY, ME and one uncapped state, from the NY registry, Maine's license list and broker pages. Days 5-10: call 20 brokers or sellers, say plainly you are forming a sponsor, and read three hypothetical bids: A, $100 with no covenant and a 60-day close; B, $97 with the Tier A covenant and a residents' association waiver of purchase rights signed up front; C, $90 with a deep covenant. Record each choice and ask for the last two sales where the seller took a lower bid for non-price reasons. Days 8-14: ask 10 residents' associations (NY, Maine) whether they would sign a purchase-right waiver for Tier A, and ask 6 allocators and DST sponsors whether a fund with a 5% ceiling at 10% gross (about 7.5% net) gets a meeting, with answers by email. Pass: at least 3 of 20 pick B or name two closed non-price discounts to a for-profit; at least 3 of 10 associations offer a waiver; at least 2 of 6 allocators ask for a deck. Kill: fewer than 3 of 20 pick B and no closed example.
result.how_critiques_were_addressed: Critique 1 (outbid, mission lane, statute, small-park economics): conceded the free label (FG Communities), outbid risk, statute commoditization and the agency-debt exclusion; corrected one point (MHAP admits for-profit acquirers with a partner, but it is a ~$24M pool); changed the debt to community banks and credit unions and the covenant to a free 5% tier plus a funded deep tier. Not answered: nothing stops FG Communities or any REIT from copying Tier A, so the moat is gone. Critique 2 (no payer, ICS died, GTM math): conceded; my rebuild shows a 4% cap costs 11-18% of price at a 7.5-8% net LP target and the parity subsidy is $66M-$210M against tens of millions of dedicated state money; split the covenant so sellers and LPs pay nothing, with the state paying only for a minority Tier B; dropped the interim-owner variant. New finding: scale lives in 100-500 site parks where institutions set price, while the covenant wins only 30-100 site parks, where $100M means 350-480 deals. Critique 3 (rates, equity, lender documents, liability): conceded; at 7.2% debt, CPI-linked caps earn 3-10% so I removed them; put the resident right to buy in a separate recorded instrument; moved equity to DST, retail and family-office channels that small-park platforms use; restricted buys to parks with municipal water and sewer and budgeted $1-2k a site for capex. Net result: every fix removes the covenant as a source of advantage, leaving an undifferentiated small-park roll-up capped by sponsor capital and track record, so I set alive to false rather than shrink it to a boutique.

remaining_holes: The core 'why pay us' question is unanswered. The pitch sells 'execution with the CFO behind it', but the CFO is the client, so the missing ingredient is one the buyer already owns. Wave 1 also leads with low-engineering lines (licence, SaaS, hosting, support), where our funding adds nothing. The real comparators are a flat-fee diagnostic from ISG, UpperEdge or Flexera, or Redress at 25% invoiced once. The rewrite's own value claim is 'roughly parity with DIY at observed 25-30% realization'. Parity is not a reason to switch, and the edge depends on realization well above 50%, which is untested.

The price concession is cosmetic. Critique 3 said 30-35% for 3 years (about 0.9-1.05x a year's saving in total fees) was unsupported. v2 charges 30% for 3 years plus 10% for 4 more, which is 1.3x at headline, 1.1x at the 26%/8% median blend and 1.24x at the 28%/10% upside blend. The headline share fell a few points while the buyer's total take stayed the same or rose. The tail was added to fix the volume math, not the buyer's problem, and the 'adds only 12%' framing measures company revenue, not what the buyer pays. The tail is also a fee for keeping a ledger of the client's own invoices.

The dated-event wedge contradicts the fee definition. Verified reduction is the lesser of units x price and the actual net fall in that vendor's invoice. SQL Server 2016 support ended 14 Jul 2026 and Windows Server 2016 ends 12 Jan 2027. I confirmed both dates, and also that these are price-up events: SQL ESU year 1 is about 75% of licence cost, then 150% and 300% (secondary sources, unverified against Microsoft). Retiring a server there avoids new spend, so no invoice line falls. VMware repricing has per-CPU core floors and bundling (consultancy sources), so removing VMs can leave the invoice flat or higher. Under v2's own definition the fee on these triggers is near zero. The post-acquisition trigger has a similar problem: synergy targets are already in the deal model, so baseline fights return.

No new evidence was gathered. Every 'what would change my mind' item from the critics is converted into a plan. The 700-payer count, 9-11.5% verified reduction, CFO acceptance of 26-30% for 3 years plus a tail, tech E&O availability, lender terms at 12% or less and client acceptance of a liability cap all remain unverified. The rewrite's own sizing, 'if under 500, the upside fails', rests on a number it admits it made up.

The 14-day test is weak and does not test the riskiest assumption. It uses a convenience sample of friendly IT-finance and ITAM contacts, and getting three companies to hand over AP exports and SSO logs by cold outreach within 7 days is unlikely. A non-sharing outcome is relabelled 'inconclusive' and a 'demand signal'. The pass metric is business owners emailing back 'agree' to a contact with no budget authority, which is stated intent, not an invoice line falling within 12 months. The real evidence (20% targeted, 5-6% realized) is about follow-through, which a 14-day email poll cannot measure.

The sales cycle and CAC are not resolved. A day-120 gate for a CFO-signed program agreement on a $40M+ base, from a new firm with no references, compares badly with Rimini's 6-12 month cycle for a simpler pitch. The Estate X-ray is 100% credited against success fees, so it is a prepayment, not revenue. The pre-sale delivery cost of $75-150k still exists and is recouped only if the deal signs. 'Pre-sale cost disappears' is overstated.

Moat and liability fixes are asserted, not shown. The outcome-statistics 'cornered resource' relies on contract language giving us ownership of derivatives, while enterprise buyers are inserting no-training and no-derivative clauses. Flexera, ISG and any firm executing retirements would accumulate the same statistics. SOC 1 Type 2 for SOX-scope systems is replaced by 'SOC 2 early', and the 6-12 month observation window is absent from the day-120 and month-12 gates. Client acceptance of a liability cap on production-affecting retirements is assumed.

The pool cross-check is mismatched. It divides by a $40B offshore run-related pool that includes the labor and AMS spend v2 says it will not claim. The headline inputs also do not reconcile with the stated per-client fees: the upside inputs give about $2.6M a year per client against the stated $1.6M peak, so the model has unstated haircuts.

The central case is a thin-margin $17M-revenue services firm that burns about $28M, with a 2-4% unconditional chance of reaching $100M. As a venture that is negative expected value unless the early gates are cheap, so everything rests on the kill gates being enforced. A plain contingent services business is valued low (PRGX comp, about $195M on roughly $165M revenue).
result.which_critiques_were_dodged_not_answered: Genuinely answered, mostly by retreat: the vendor-labor lever is abandoned, so fixed-price vendors and AI pass-through no longer matter. The SAP custom-code wedge is dropped. The Big 4 co-sign is withdrawn over SEC independence risk. The 36-month annuity volume math is reproduced and conceded. The roughly 50 largest in-sourcers are excluded. A dollars-per-invoice-line unit of account replaces the baseline fight. Accounts under $40M are refused, and funding is gated at an 18-month payback. Dodged or only cosmetically answered: (1) Critique 1 point 3, the contested-band argument. The rewrite moves its lead to client-controlled lines (licences, hosting, retirement), exactly where Redress, Flexera, ISG and Vendr-type firms already sit. The dossier's own pivot note called this a real but smaller and more contested wedge. The only answer is 'we fund the engineering', and the low-engineering sequencing removes that. The sponsor channel is still asserted, not owned, and Redress already claims 14 PE portfolio companies. (2) Critiques 2 and 3 on in-house work and falling engineering cost. 'We sell the sweep and guarantee, not code' just restates that the bottleneck is organizational, which is the client's job. It does not explain why a CFO who has already backed the program pays 1.1-1.3x annual savings instead of a flat fee or in-house work. (3) Critique 3 on price. The headline share fell 4-9 points, but the tail raised the total take. (4) Critique 2 on sales cycle and CAC. 'Cash in month 2-4' is a credited prepayment, not earned margin. (5) The data-library moat versus no-training clauses. The answer is to define derivatives as ours by contract, which assumes buyers concede what they are now refusing. (6) SOC 1 versus SOC 2. The control is swapped, not addressed. (7) Critique 1 point 5 on baseline disputes. Net-invoice-fall measurement reintroduces the dispute on price-up events (ESU, VMware repricing, lost volume tiers), and v2 names those events as its triggers.
result.upside_believable: No. The $100M upside needs several assumptions at once, and the author's own sensitivities show how fragile it is. About 700 reachable payers is unsourced, though the definition is broader than the dossier's 300-600 offshore-labor count, so it is not absurd. Accounts must land at $40M and double to an effective $80M within 3 years. Verified reduction must reach 9% at year 3 and 11.5% at year 5, and the rewrite concedes documented per-client savings of $1-5M a year do not support that. Blended share must be 28%, engineering cost 0.30x, and signings must climb from 3 to 20 a year via channels that are asserted, not owned. Tech E&O and cheap receivables financing must also be available. Any one adverse change drops year-7 revenue below $100M by the rewrite's own numbers: signings down 30% gives $70M, and a $60M effective base gives $76M. These assumptions are correlated, not independent, because they all depend on owner follow-through plus CFO willingness to pay a top-of-range share for a long tail. The 2-4% odds come from the author's own priors and carry no validation. Peak burn of about $32M for the upside versus about $28M for the median looks too low for 94 logos funding roughly $2.8M of engineering each. The gate-and-kill structure is honest and cheap, so the idea is worth testing as an option, but it is not a believable path to a large business as written.

result.rationale:
The insight is real. Savings that get identified but never executed, because nobody is paid to switch things off, is a true gap. The 5-6% realized against 20% targeted evidence supports it. Pricing on third-party invoice lines that actually fall is a cleaner unit of account than the usual baseline fight. The dossier also found no one selling vendor-neutral, engineering-funded, invoice-verified retirement. But the idea is weak as a seed-stage venture bet, for four reasons.

1. The economics are unconvincing. A CFO who has already backed the program pays about 1.1-1.3x a year's savings in fees, and the author's own value claim is "roughly parity with DIY". The tail was added to fix the company's volume math, not the buyer's problem. Wave 1 leads with low-engineering lines (licence, SaaS, hosting, support), where funding adds nothing. Those lines are also where Redress (25% of savings), Flexera, ISG and in-house teams already sit.

2. The dated-event wedge contradicts the fee definition. SQL Server and Windows Server end-of-support and VMware repricing are price-up events. Retiring a server there avoids new spend, so no invoice line falls and the fee is near zero. Post-merger synergies are already in the deal model, so baseline fights return.

3. The numbers describe a thin-margin services firm. The median is about $17M revenue with about $28M burned. The author puts odds of $100M at 2-4%, and it fails if any single assumption moves. Contingent services revenue is valued low (PRGX sold for about $195M). Capital needs are venture-sized but the margins are services-grade. That is a decent small business, not a Stripe, Toast or Samsara.

4. Demand is unproven and the moat is thin. There is no RFP, no LOI and no precedent of a vendor-neutral third party collecting a share of audited run savings. The 700-payer count is invented, and the 14-day test measures stated intent from a friendly sample, not savings that actually reach invoices. The moat is asserted at best. Outcome statistics run into no-training clauses, and competitors could accumulate the same data. Tech E&O cover for production changes by AI agents is untested.

What keeps this from a 1-2 is that the gates are cheap and honest, and the central observation about the execution gap is true. Whether it becomes a funded-execution business or a smaller, contested licence-savings business is unknown.

Prize: this is a contingent-fee services company, not software. The author's own median is about $17M revenue in year 7 with thin margins and about $28M of burn. The $100M case needs about five correlated assumptions at once: 700 reachable payers (unsourced), accounts doubling to $80M, 9-11.5% verified reduction, 28% share and 20 signings a year. The author puts it at 2-4% unconditional. The closest scaled comp, PRGX, sold for about $195M, and Ameresco runs about 12% EBITDA on a heavy balance sheet. A seed fund needs a credible path to a $1B+ outcome, and this offers a tiny tail. It is a decent small business with an unusually honest kill-gate plan, and that honesty lowers the venture score because it confirms the ceiling.

Why-now: the reasons are moderate and mixed. AI lowers retirement engineering cost, but the same tools are cheap for clients, who can do the work in-house (Citi). CFO pressure for AI offsets and the lack of a neutral referee for AI savings (ISG) are real. The dated-event wedge undercuts itself. SQL Server and Windows Server end-of-support and VMware repricing are price-up events, so under v2's own fee definition (the lesser of units removed times price and the actual net fall in the invoice) the invoice line often does not fall. The SAP wedge was already dropped. The post-acquisition trigger runs into synergy numbers already in the deal model, which brings back baseline fights.

Originality: the slot of vendor-neutral, funded, paid only on an invoice-line drop is genuinely open, and no ESCO-for-IT exists. But the dossier warns it may be open because the economics are hard. The critics also showed that the pitch is crowded: Redress, Flexera, ISG, Rimini, AMS self-funding and AI-SRE vendors all sit nearby. The unit-of-account fix (units times price, not baseline) is a clever design, not a non-consensus insight about the world.

Feasibility: this is the weakest point. The customer must have a CFO sign, owners release spend, Internal Audit accept the ledger and the client's change process execute, and the firm must carry production-change liability with unproven E&O cover and no SOC 1 path. The evidence for realization is bad (20% targeted, 5-6% realized). The sales cycle is likely 9-18 months for a new firm with no references, and the Estate X-ray is credited, so it is a prepayment and not margin. The 14-day test cannot measure follow-through, which is the riskiest assumption. Capital need is heavy ($28-60M) against equity-like receivables.

Defensibility: no power is strong at launch. Counter-positioning holds only against AMS vendors. The outcome-statistics moat conflicts with no-training and no-derivative clauses. Flexera, ISG and any executing firm can collect the same statistics. The ledger as standard is speculative. The tail adds only about 12% to revenue and is a fee for keeping a record of the client's own invoices.

Demand: there is no RFP, precedent or CFO letter showing anyone will pay 26-30% for 3 years plus a 10% tail. That is about 1.1-1.3x annual savings, versus Redress at 25% once or a flat-fee diagnostic. The v2 value claim is roughly parity with doing it yourself. The only quantified evidence on follow-through is negative. Zero validation has been gathered; every critic request was converted into a plan.

Net: a thoughtful, well-gated small services bet that a seed fund would pass on. A pass is the correct call unless an early gate (owner release above 50% of identified dollars plus CFO sign at 25%+ share) is cleared first.

Scored as a serial founder of profitable companies. This is a decent small business at best, not venture-scale.

PAIN: Cost-out is a real CFO theme. Event-driven entry (post-merger synergy windows, pre-exit EBITDA, end-of-support) is the best part of the refined idea. But retiring applications is chronic and important, not urgent. The dossier's one realization data point is a 20% target that delivered 5-6%, and business owners resist. The refined idea names owner release of funds as its riskiest assumption and has not tested it.

FIRST 10 CUSTOMERS IN 6-12 MONTHS: The paid Estate X-ray ($75-150k, 100% credited) can plausibly win a few buyers, and PE operating partners and integration offices are reachable. But a CFO-signed program agreement with a 30% share for 3 years plus a tail, from a firm with no references, will probably take 9-18 months. First success-fee dollars arrive around month 9-15 at best. The critic is right that the credited X-ray is prepayment, not margin, and that pre-sale delivery cost still exists.

UNIT ECONOMICS: These are weak and fragile. The buyer pays about 1.1-1.3x a year's savings for work that is roughly parity with doing it yourself, so the 'why pay us' question is unanswered. The wedge also contradicts the fee definition. SQL Server and Windows Server end-of-support and VMware repricing are price-up events, so retiring units there avoids new spend rather than dropping an invoice line. Under the idea's own definition, the fee on those triggers is near zero. Engineering is funded up front against disputable, contingent receivables, valued like PRGX (about $195M on about $165M of revenue). The model's own median is $17M of revenue in year 7 with about $28M of burn, which is poor capital efficiency. The upside needs about 700 payers (unsourced), accounts that double, 9-11.5% reduction (documented savings are $1-5M per client, which does not support that), and 20 signings a year. Any one miss drops year-7 revenue below $100M, and the author puts the odds at 2-4%.

WHAT IS GOOD: Real, honest gating. A cheap 14-day test, plus kill gates at day 60, day 120 and month 12. A defensible unit of account (a third-party invoice line that falls). The slot between Redress, Flexera, ISG and the AMS vendors is genuinely unoccupied. The ledger could become a standard. The X-ray is a legitimate consulting wedge that could fund a small profitable firm.

WHAT IS BAD: Moat is weak. Counter-positioning holds only against AMS vendors on scope removal. The outcome-statistics moat conflicts with buyers' no-training and no-derivative clauses. Incumbents and AI tooling make execution cheap for clients. SOC 1 timing, liability caps and tech E&O are unproven, and no new evidence was gathered; every open item became a plan. Demand evidence is thin: no RFPs, no LOIs, no precedent for a vendor-neutral party paid a share of application run savings for 3 years or more.

Seed-stage calibration: a 4 means decent but not a deal top funds would compete for. As a serial founder I would run the 14-day test because it costs about nothing. I would not commit capital to the funded-retirement model before seeing signed CFO paper.

remaining_holes: The scale arithmetic measures the wrong denominator. The rewrite says 22-35 parks a year is 5-8% of Berkadia's 460 national sales, but its own wedge is six states (NY, ME, NJ, WA, OR, MA). Those states hold roughly 3,000-5,000 parks (NY 1,167 and ME 475 are from the dossier; NJ ~179, MA ~85, OR ~1,000-1,400 and WA 700-2,000 come from low-quality or conflicting sources). At Berkadia's ~1% turnover that is about 40-50 trades a year across the six states, and only a minority fall in the 40-150 site band. Even at 3% turnover, 22-35 wins a year would be a large share of all eligible trades, in states where residents can match the bid. This is my arithmetic with assumed turnover, but the rewrite never tests it, and it is probably the largest unaddressed hole. FG's pace was built in uncapped, no-ROFR NC/SC/VA, which the wedge states are not.

The two-week test cannot answer the critics' own falsifier. Critics 1 and 2 said stated willingness would not count and asked for at least 3 signed LOIs or accepted bids within about 5% of a market bid. The rewrite rules out LOIs and runs a hypothetical A/B/C bid question on 20 brokers. Brokers owe the seller a fiduciary duty and pay no cost for saying B in a survey. The pass bar of 3 of 20 is low. The only revealed-preference piece is the request for two closed non-price discounts to a for-profit buyer.

The pricing is internally inconsistent. Tier A is described as a covenant that 'costs sellers nothing', yet the bid is up to 3% below the best uncovenanted offer. The 5% ceiling is also looser than the statutory defaults in the wedge states (NY 3% default with a 6% ceiling, NJ 3.5%, WA 5%). The price-parity result (-6.5% to +0.6% against institutions) is close to tautological, because a 5% ceiling barely binds against 5.5% market rent growth. A covenant that barely binds is worth nothing to the seller, the residents or the state. The rewrite concedes this ('a label any competitor can copy') but still bases the bid on it.

Revenue is mixed between two definitions. The $8M median and $60M upside are consolidated park rent. The rewrite's own sponsor economics (1.5% asset-management fee plus carry, 5-8% of rent) put a GP-style sponsor's revenue near $3-5M in the upside case. The fund/DST/family-office structure it proposes does not consolidate rent the way FG Communities does.

The median case is not consistent with the rest of the rewrite. $8M of rent is about 1,100-1,400 sites. That exceeds the dossier's own shrink-to-survive range ($1-6M, 3-8 subsidized parks). It also assumes the co-founder and the fund close that the upside list treats as requirements. A median for a dead idea should be close to zero.

The upside's equity figure uses the best case. The $165M raise is built on $22k of equity a site (65% LTV). The rewrite says agency debt is unavailable to small parks. FG's FY2025 Form C-AR shows notes payable of $84.8M against $200M of assets (about 42%) and $115M of equity for about 3,100 sites (about $37k a site). At that ratio, 7,450 sites need about $300M, which the rewrite mentions but does not use in the upside row.

Rent growth of 4.5% a year is assumed for a portfolio concentrated in states with a 3% (NY) or 3.5% (NJ) default cap, plus a Maine mediation right above CPI+1% and a 5% self-imposed ceiling. NY allows up to 6% only with justification.

The exit and covenant-enforcement questions from critic 3 are not re-answered. These are whether a lender accepts a resident right to buy outside the lease, whether a recorded cap survives foreclosure, and who buys in years 7-10 when ROC USA deploys about $26M a year. The rewrite moved the purchase right into a separate instrument but did not test any of this. The claim that community banks and credit unions finance small parks is partly supported (FG's Form C-AR shows 3.25-8% bank and credit-union notes), but the LTV, tenor and rate available to a first-time sponsor are untested.

The rewrite's description of FG Communities is slightly off. The Nasdaq entity (FGC, formerly FG Nexus, an Ethereum treasury company) holds a minority stake and is evaluating a combination. The operating company, FG Communities Inc., is a private Nevada corporation that has raised about $133M of Series A preferred under Reg D since Dec 2022. Its founders include a former TD Ameritrade chairman and a 95-community MHC operator. The comparable's capital channel and brand are not what a first-time sponsor can replicate. The rewrite says this in one clause ('a team a new founder does not have') but the upside pace still leans on it.
result.which_critiques_were_dodged_not_answered:
Mostly conceded rather than dodged. Concessions that hold up: free-label copyability (FG Communities), statute commoditizing the covenant, agency-debt exclusion, no payer for a deep cap at scale, and the 4% parity subsidy exceeding state money. PRICE at zero for FY2026 is likely but not fully confirmed. The rewrite's correction of critic 1 on NY MHAP is right: the term sheet says eligible applicants include mission-driven organizations 'whether not-for-profit or for-profit', with a hire-or-partner experience rule. The rewrite is also right that the pool is small and capped at the as-is appraisal, so it cannot fund an overbid. Its FG numbers check out against FG Communities Inc.'s FY2025 Form C-AR: $9.6M rental income and about 3,100 sites at year-end. Banks and credit unions do finance its parks, at 3.25-8%.

Dodged or only half-answered:
1. Critics 1 and 2 named signed LOIs or accepted bids at no more than 5% below a market bid as the thing that would change their minds. The rewrite swaps in a hypothetical broker survey and rules out LOIs.
2. The 5-8%-of-national-sales framing answers critic 2's 'about 5% of national trades' objection by restating it, while the wedge is now six states where the share would be far higher.
3. Critic 3's covenant-versus-lender-documents and exit-buyer points were handled by moving the purchase right into a separate instrument, with no evidence that lenders or buyers accept that structure.
4. Critic 3's point that rate shocks hurt a capped buyer is answered by dropping CPI-linked caps and adopting a loose 5% ceiling. That fixes the IRR but empties the covenant of value, which is the rewrite's own conclusion.
5. The new 'FG Communities reaches the same niche' claim is used as a benchmark for the upside rather than as evidence that the market is closed to a copycat.
result.upside_believable: Partly. The $60M upside is an extrapolation of a real comparable. FG Communities Inc. reached $9.6M of 2025 rent on about 3,100 sites in about 3.5 years, then about 4,000 sites by Sep 2026. Its recent pace of 900-1,900 sites a year is not outlandish, and the path to about 7,450 sites and about $60M of rent is internally consistent arithmetic. I do not find it believable as a Covenant Parks outcome, for these reasons. (1) The comparable's pace was built in uncapped, no-ROFR Southeastern markets with a very large pool of small parks. The wedge is six capped or ROFR states, where the same acquisition pace would be a large fraction of all eligible trades. My rough estimate is 15-50 or more eligible trades a year, so winning 22-35 a year looks implausible, and residents can match any bid. (2) The comparable's money came from about $133M of Reg D preferred and a founder team with a TD Ameritrade-level brand. A first-time sponsor's 1031/DST, retail and family-office route is not shown to exist. (3) The row uses $22k of equity a site, not FG's observed $37-40k. At FG's ratio the same $60M needs about $300M. (4) The 4.5% rent growth assumption exceeds the NY and NJ default caps. (5) $60M is consolidated park rent, and a GP-style sponsor would earn about 5-8% of it. (6) The upside needs all seven stated assumptions at once, and the rewrite itself puts the $100M row at low single-digit probability. The $8M median is not credible next to a verdict of dead, because it is above the dossier's own $1-6M realistic range.

result.rationale:
I read the full dossier and weighed the refined pitch, the second-round critic and the three original critiques. The refined idea is a real-estate sponsor, not a venture company. A seed partner would pass on it.

Size of prize: The land-lease community market is large (about 4.3M sites, a $25-40B annual lot-rent pool). But the reachable slice is small. The wedge is 30-41 site parks in capped or purchase-right states, where winning means 350-480 deals for $100M of rent. Institutions set the price in the 100-500 site core. The pitch's own upside is about $60M of consolidated park rent by year 11. It needs seven assumptions to hold at once and about $165-300M of equity. The pitch itself puts the $100M row at low single-digit probability. Consolidated rent is also the wrong revenue measure. A GP-style sponsor earns about 5-8% of it, roughly $3-5M, which makes this a boutique fund-manager outcome. Median case: the pitch's $8M of rent is higher than the dossier's own $1-6M realistic range, so even that figure is generous.

Why-now: The trigger is real. Purchase-right and rent-cap statutes have spread (NY, ME, NJ, WA, OR), REIT rent growth of 5-9% and 23% institutional ownership have made owners politically exposed, and a few for-profits will take a recorded covenant when a grant pays for it (Minnesota). But the dossier shows the benefit goes to nonprofits and co-ops first, since the seller tax credits and HUD/Fannie incentives exclude for-profits. Statute delivers the covenant free, which commoditizes it. The 10-year yield is near 5.1% and agency-range debt near 7.2%, which hurts a capped buyer most. Timing therefore works against this particular wedge.

Non-consensus and right: The covenant-as-differentiator insight was interesting, and the dossier found no for-profit with a recorded rent covenant at scale. But the stress test showed why the gap exists. The free tier is a label FG Communities or any REIT can copy. The deep tier (a 4% cap) has no payer at scale: parity subsidy is $66-210M against tens of millions of state money. The last open question is whether a seller with a market bid will take a covenant bid within 3% of it. The evidence leans no (Fox Run, Cascade Acres, the Maine ROFR failures). The Tier A price-parity result is also close to tautological, because a 5% ceiling barely binds against about 5.5% market rent growth, so it is worth little to anyone.

Feasibility and defensibility: Execution needs a seasoned manufactured-home-community operator as co-founder, an unproven 1031/DST/retail/family-office capital channel, and community-bank debt for a first-time sponsor. Agency debt excludes the small parks. There is no durable moat. The comparable (FG Communities Inc.) had about $133M of Reg D preferred, a founder team with a major brokerage-chairman-level brand, and uncapped southeastern markets without purchase rights.

Evidence of demand: Residents want the protection, but no seller, lender or allocator has been found who will pay for a for-profit covenant. The nearest attempt (ROC USA's ICS) completed one deal and was shut down in 2025. The proposed two-week test is a hypothetical broker survey, not signed LOIs.

Net: A decent small business or boutique fund for an experienced operator, not venture-scale. A 3 is the right calibration.

This is a decent small real-estate sponsorship business, not a venture-scale company. I scored the opportunity, not the polish, and the refined version removes most of what made the original interesting.

Insight and timing (originality 5, timing 5): The 2025-26 shift is real. Purchase-right and rent-cap statutes are passing in NY, ME, NJ, WA and OR, REITs are raising rents 5-9%, and institutions now hold about 23% of the market. The contrarian idea is a for-profit that records a rent-ceiling covenant and sells it as a seller or lender advantage. That is non-obvious, and the dossier found no for-profit doing it. But the refined version admits the free 5% tier is a label anyone can copy. FG Communities already occupies the same small-park niche with the same mission language. The ceiling also barely binds, since NY and NJ statutory defaults are 3-3.5% and market rent growth is about 5.5%. Statute delivers the covenant for free where it applies. The subsidy and tax breaks go to nonprofits and co-ops, so the shift favors ROC USA first. A why-now that favors a competitor is only half a why-now.

Upside and defensibility (upside 3, defensibility 2): This is a capital-bound roll-up, so scale depends on equity raised, not on product or network effects. The author puts the $100M-revenue outcome at low single-digit probability. The $60M upside is consolidated park rent, which needs about 7,450 sites and $165M to $300M of equity, and a fund-style sponsor would earn only 5-8% of that rent. The median of $8M exceeds the dossier's own realistic range of $1-6M. Two things limit scale. The sellers are mostly one-park owners with 30-41 sites. Institutions set the price in the 100-500 site parks where the volume is. The deep-cap tier has no payer: parity costs $66-210M against tens of millions of state money. Counter-positioning is gone, and none of the 7 Powers is reachable in time.

Demand evidence (3): There is real political and resident demand. Minnesota and NY MHAP show a state will pay for a recorded cap. Against that, the dossier found no seller, broker, lender or allocator who says they will pay for a for-profit covenant. The one documented contested sale (Cascade Acres) saw a private-equity bid about 20% over appraisal. Maine's co-op offers were beaten on speed and terms. ROC's ICS, the closest attempt, completed one deal and was shut down. The two-week test is a hypothetical broker survey, which is weak.

Feasibility (3): A first-time founder cannot meet the agency-debt sponsor rules, so the idea needs a seasoned MHC operator as co-founder. Rates are hostile, with the 10-year around 5.1% and debt around 7.2%. Right-of-first-refusal laws let residents match any covenant bid. Lender rules against purchase options in leases, and covenant survival on foreclosure, are untested. Exit buyers are thin. What remains is a boutique mission-aligned small-park sponsor.

Seed-stage comparison: a fundable-by-friends vehicle for a specific experienced operator, not something top funds would compete for.

This fails on the tests I use as a serial founder. There is no urgent, budgeted pain. Residents pay nothing extra. Sellers have market bids in hand and historically take the higher, cleaner offer: at Fox Run the co-op bid was higher and still lost on terms and speed, and Cascade Acres drew a PE overbid of about 20%. The only documented budget line is state money for nonprofits and co-ops, roughly $24M for NY MHAP and tens of millions elsewhere. The dossier and both critics found no seller, lender or allocator who says they will pay for a for-profit covenant. The idea's own refinement concedes the free 5% tier is a label that FG Communities or any REIT can copy. It also concedes the deep tier has no payer at scale: parity costs $66M-$210M against state money in the tens of millions, and PRICE funding is zero for FY2026. Once the covenant stops being an advantage, what remains is an undifferentiated small-park roll-up, which is a real-estate sponsor business and not a software-style company.

First 10 customers: a customer here is an acquired park, and each one needs $1-3M or more of equity, a sponsor track record, and in NY or Maine a 60-140 day purchase-right window in which residents can match the bid. A first-time sponsor cannot meet Freddie's two-year-experience rule, and fund formation takes about 18-22 months. The realistic path is 3-8 subsidized parks and $1-6M of rent, which the dossier itself states and which sits below the stated $8M median.

Unit economics and timing: with the 10-year near 5.1% and agency-range debt around 7.2%, leverage is negative. Rebuilt IRRs for a capped owner are 3-10% on the CPI-linked cases. Fixed-cap cases near 10-12% depend on a mild exit. Rent growth is pinned below expense growth in capped states (NY 3%, NJ 3.5%), which squeezes the sponsor. Capital is not efficient: about $22k-$37k of equity per site.

Scale: $100M of rent needs 350-480 deals of 30-41 sites in six states with only about 40-50 trades a year, and the $60M upside needs all seven assumptions to hold at once. Sponsor revenue (fee plus carry, 5-8% of rent) is only about $3-5M even in that case. Defensibility is nil, since there is no moat from regulation, capital, brand or process. FG Communities, ROC USA, Havenpark and the REITs already occupy the lanes.

Credit: the political tailwind is real, and a seasoned MHC operator could run a modest, decent small-park business in this niche. That caps it at a small-business outcome, not a venture-scale or even a differentiated one. The covenant premise was tested hard and mostly died, so this scores 2.
